CHAPTER I INTRODUCTION

These are plain common sense business questions, predicated on our present oil requirements as an esta'blished fact, and on the suggested possibility that our prodigal spending of our petroleum heritage may cause its too rapid depletion if not its early exhaustion in the midst of our spendthrift career, and at some untoward moment send us beggars to foreign countries for the precious fluid necessary not only to satisfy our extravagance but, even to sustain our industrial prosperity, our standards of'iving and our civilization. The American struggle for a share in Middle East

oil exploitation in the 1920s has become one of'pecial 
signif'icance in the 1970s. Recent. demonstrations of 
American dependency on Arab oil have dominated the formu 
lation of both foreign and domestic policy. David White's 
dismal prediction, only one of many made in the early 
twenties, has returned to haunt us with the specter of' 
crumbling way of life. 
As a result of the current energy crisis, much has 
been written concerning the Middle East and American oil 
policy. However, there are surprisingly few definitive

works concerning the manner in which American participation in Middle East oil exploitation (the first step toward the pr esent dependency) was initially accomplished. Even those scholarly efforts which treat with the subject do so as part of'roader studies.

This thesis will examine that point at which the first penetration of the area by American oil companies occurred and, specifically, the relationship between United States foreign policy and American business in this regard. By approaching the subject in this manner, the thrust of the inquiry is considerably narrowed. Only the specific geographic point of exploitative penetration, Mesopotamia, the area which currently comprises the state of Iraq, and, particularly, the northern provinces of Mosul and Baghdad, will be addressed. Oil exploitation by Americans in the Middle East was virtually non-existent prior to the con clusion of'he final working agreement between the American Group of'il companies and the Turkish Petroleum Company in 1928.

Yet, in this single episode can be found several of *he major principles underlying *he foreign policy and energy questions of the present. For example, while the Chief'xecutive, in concert with Congress, is responsible for the formulation of foreign policy, in the absence of clear leadership that function will fall to the Secretary of State. Furthermore, if foreign policy is not executed by official represen*atives of *he Government, diplomacy will be conducted by private individuals who are active in the international sphere. It is also *rue that a state will permit practices which are ethically questionable in the light of its own s*ated principles provided those practices satisf'y an urgent requirement, as in the case of virtual oil monopoly in the Middle East being accepted as a means of acquiring crude oil stocks. If this respon sibili*y of'overnment to choose *he lesser of two evils in order to avert a perceived threat *o the national well being becomes clear in the struggle for Middle East oil, it becomes no less evident that the responsibility of businessmen is to their stockholders. Thus, it will be demonstrated that, contrary to the popular image of the entrepreneur, big, established businesses are not com fortable with the role of risk taker. They seek to attain the greatest profit with the least possible danger to invested capital. The efforts of the State Department on behalf of American oilmen in this endeavor are indicative of the importance that the United States, Government attached to the open door principle. More importantly, examination of the contest demonstrates the true character of that principle. In s*ripping away the illusion of altruism with which American leaders sought to cloak the open door, one uncovers the structure of a coldly practical and

e ffec tive diplomatic strategy. The heart of'he open door principle, as stated, was that the economic activity of'he world and the opportunity thereto should be determined 'by free com petition, unfettered by national politics. However, in

Mesopotamia, it was applied as a lever to open an exclu sive foreign commercial domain to exploitation by American interests. 2

Following World War I, the British and French divided former Ottoman territory between them. In fact, discussions concerning such division began soon after the out'break of'he war. France sought domination of'he Levant; England aspired to leadership and control of a new Islamic empire which would permit her to straddle the Middle East and provide a geographical link with her Indian empire. The Sykes-Picot agreement, in 1916, divided the region into French, British and international zones,

designated in blue, red and brown, respectively. Subzones, designated "a" for French domination and "b" for British, were reserved for the creation of puppet Arab states or confederations. Mesopotamia (Iraq) and Palestine were to be administered by the British; Syria and Lebanon, by the

undertake to grant to the French Government or its nominee 25 per cent. of the net output of crude oil at current market rates which His Majesty's Government may secure from the Mesopotamian oil fields, in the event of'heir being developed by Government action; or in the event of a private petroleum company being used to develop the Mesopotamian oil fields, the British Government will place at the disposal of the French Government a share of'5 per cent. in such company. The price to be paid for such participation to be no more than that, paid by any of the other participants to the said petro leum company. Virtually all of these arrangements were made in secret, but information came to American representatives in bits and pieces, or was ferreted out by men like Leland

Summers of the American Commission to the Paris peace 
conference in 1919. Summers badgered members of the British 
Delegation into admitting the existence of these covert 
negotiations, then doggedly forced assurances from the 
British that exclusion of the United States was not in 
tended. The British, of course, were less than candid in 
giving these assurances. 
Complicating the issue was the boasting of British 
oilmen that they had cornered the petroleum supply of'he 
world. In 1919, for example, Sir Edward Mackay Edgar, of 
Venezuelan Oil Concessions, Ltd., announced that the 
American oil industry had "recklessly squandered in 
sixty years a legacy which . . . should have lasted 
at least a century and a half." This was exactly 
what many concerned Americans had been saying since the 
turn of'he century. There had been a growing uneasiness
